passage:
In Class 4B of the municipal school in Pune, Ramesh sir noticed that Naveen knew almost every answer and shouted most of them first. He tapped his pencil, tipped his chair and was out of his seat six times in one maths period.
Some staff-room voices called him a menace. Ramesh sir didn't. Instead he moved Naveen near the window, made him the board cleaner so he could get up between lessons, and gave him a small card to hold up instead of calling out.
Things improved, but not completely. So at the parent meeting he spoke to Naveen's mother gently. 'He's bright and trying hard. If you think it would help, the school counsellor can suggest where to get a proper assessment. It's only to understand him better.'

qa.q: What job did Ramesh sir give Naveen?
qa.a: Board cleaner, so he could get up between lessons.

qa.q: How did Ramesh sir feel about Naveen, unlike some staff-room voices?
qa.a: He felt patient and hopeful about Naveen, seeing him as bright and trying hard rather than a menace.

qa.q: What choice did Ramesh sir make when things improved but not completely?
qa.a: He gently raised with Naveen's mother that the school counsellor could suggest where to get a proper assessment, only to understand Naveen better.

qa.q: How might Naveen's mother feel hearing her son called bright and trying hard?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and less defensive, and more open to an assessment because it came with respect, not blame.

grounding: Shows a teacher who sees a bright, restless pupil, adjusts seating and gives movement breaks instead of labelling, and gently suggests a professional assessment.

passage:
'Seven eights are fifty-six!' Divyansh shouted before Hansa Ma'am had finished the question.
'Right, Divyansh. Next time, hand up first. Can you try?'
'Sorry, Ma'am. It just jumps out.'
Ten minutes later he was standing by the window. 'Ma'am, can I sharpen my pencil?'
'You've sharpened it twice already.' She smiled. 'Tell you what. Be my messenger. Take this note to the office and back. Then sit and finish four sums.'
'Really?' He was already at the door.
When he came back, he finished all four sums, fast.
At home time Hansa Ma'am said, 'Divyansh, I'd like to talk to your Papa tomorrow. Nothing bad. Just how to help you learn best, maybe with advice from someone trained in this.'
'Am I in trouble?'
'No. You're clever. I want to help.'

qa.q: What answer did Divyansh shout out?
How does Hansa Ma'am feel about Divyansh's blurting and restlessness?
qa.a: She feels patient and caring rather than annoyed; she smiles, makes him her messenger and wants to help him learn best.

qa.q: What choice did Hansa Ma'am make when Divyansh was out of his seat again?
qa.a: She made him her messenger to the office, giving him a movement break, and afterwards he finished four sums fast.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel when Hansa Ma'am says 'You're clever. I want to help'?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and trusted, since he was afraid he was in trouble.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a bright pupil who blurts and cannot sit still, giving movement breaks rather than labels, and planning to talk with the family about expert advice.
